questions.stem: Which is a key role of operations management?
options: choosing which advertising channels will reach the business's target market
ensuring goods and services are produced at the right cost, quality and time
deciding how the business's profits will be divided among its shareholders
negotiating the enterprise agreement that sets employees' pay and conditions
questions.explanation: Operations management plans and controls the production of goods and services so that they meet targets for cost, quality and timing. Negotiating pay is a human resources role.

questions.stem: The operations objective of dependability means:
options: consistently delivering products and services as promised
producing goods and services at the lowest possible cost
changing products or volumes quickly to suit customers
making goods that meet or exceed the required standard
questions.explanation: Dependability is reliability: doing things on time and as promised every time. Changing products or volumes to suit customers is flexibility.

questions.stem: A Sydney print shop promises to have posters ready within two hours of an order being placed. Which operations objective is it emphasising?
options: quality
flexibility
speed
cost
questions.explanation: Speed is the time taken between a customer's order and delivery. A short, fixed turnaround time is a speed objective.

questions.stem: A Newcastle furniture maker builds each table to the customer's chosen size, timber and finish. Which operations objective does this mainly reflect?
options: speed
cost
flexibility
dependability
questions.explanation: Flexibility is the ability to vary products, mix or volume to meet customer needs, as in making each table to order. Dependability is about delivering reliably as promised.

questions.stem: A budget airline cuts the time its planes spend at the gate and offers no free meals or seat changes. Which trade-off between operations objectives does this show?
options: it favours low cost and speed at the expense of flexibility
it favours flexibility and quality at the expense of speed
it favours dependability at the expense of both cost and speed
it favours quality at the expense of cost and dependability
questions.explanation: Standardising the service and turning planes around quickly keeps costs low, but customers have fewer choices, so flexibility is reduced. The airline is clearly not sacrificing speed.

questions.stem: A Wollongong bakery decides to bake every loaf to order so that customers can choose any grain and size. Which trade-off is most likely?
options: lower cost per loaf, but lower quality and less dependability
faster service, but less flexibility and a narrower product range
higher dependability, but much lower flexibility and quality
higher flexibility, but higher cost per loaf and slower service
questions.explanation: Customising every order increases flexibility but reduces the efficiency of batch baking, so costs rise and customers wait longer. Operations objectives often conflict, so managers choose which to prioritise.

questions.stem: A product layout arranges equipment and workers:
options: around a product that stays in one place while it is built
in a mixture of departments and production lines
in the sequence of steps needed to make a standardised product
in departments that each perform one type of task
questions.explanation: A product (line) layout follows the order of production steps, suiting high volumes of a standard product, such as a bottling line. Departments grouped by task form a functional layout.

questions.stem: A hospital groups its X-ray, pathology and surgery services in separate areas, and each patient moves between them as needed. Which layout is this?
options: fixed-position layout
hybrid layout
functional layout
product layout
questions.explanation: A functional (process) layout groups similar equipment and skills together, suiting varied work where each customer or job follows its own route. A product layout follows one fixed sequence.

questions.stem: Which business is most likely to use a fixed-position layout?
options: a machine shop with lathe and welding areas
a shipbuilder constructing a ferry
a soft-drink bottling plant
a supermarket checkout area
questions.explanation: In a fixed-position layout the product stays in one place and workers, materials and equipment come to it, as with ships, bridges and buildings. A bottling plant suits a product layout.

questions.stem: A Penrith factory makes standard parts on a production line, while a separate area groups machines by type for custom orders. Which layout is this?
options: hybrid layout
functional layout
product layout
fixed-position layout
questions.explanation: A hybrid layout combines elements of two or more layouts, here a production line and a functional area. Using either one alone would not describe the whole factory.

questions.stem: Which is the main disadvantage of a product layout compared with a functional layout?
options: it has a higher cost per unit when large volumes are produced
it requires every worker to have a wide range of different skills
it is unsuited to producing large volumes of a standard product
it is inflexible, and a fault at one step can stop the whole line
questions.explanation: Because each step depends on the one before, product layouts are hard to change and vulnerable to breakdowns. They usually give the lowest cost per unit at high volumes, not the highest.

questions.stem: A café moves its coffee machine closer to the counter and creates a clear path between the kitchen and tables. This layout optimisation mainly aims to:
options: increase the café's fixed costs to raise its prices
change the café from a functional to a fixed layout
meet the legal requirement to have a product layout
improve the flow of work and reduce wasted movement
questions.explanation: Layout optimisation arranges space to improve the flow of work, staff and customer safety, and customer convenience. There is no legal requirement to use any particular layout type.

questions.stem: A warehouse marks walkways for staff and separates them from forklift lanes. This layout decision mainly improves:
options: product flexibility
safety
speed of delivery
customer convenience
questions.explanation: Separating people from moving machinery reduces the risk of injury, which is a safety goal of layout optimisation and supports WHS obligations.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart is used in operations to show:
options: each task's start date, duration and deadline along a timeline
the volume of output needed to cover fixed and variable costs
the percentage of maximum capacity currently being used
the stages of a product from introduction to decline
questions.explanation: A Gantt chart shows tasks as horizontal bars along a timeline, so managers can see when each starts, how long it lasts and whether it meets its deadline. The output needed to cover costs is the break-even point.

questions.stem: On a Gantt chart for a shop fit-out, the painting bar starts at the beginning of day 6 and lasts 4 days, and its deadline is the end of day 12. Which statement is correct?
options: painting ends on day 9, one day after its deadline
painting ends on day 9, three days before its deadline
painting ends on day 10, two days before its deadline
painting ends on day 12, exactly on its deadline
questions.explanation: Starting on day 6 and lasting 4 days covers days 6, 7, 8 and 9, so painting ends on day 9, three days before the day-12 deadline. Adding 6 + 4 without counting the start day gives day 10.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines the critical path of a project?
options: the list of tasks that can be delayed without affecting the finish date
the order in which tasks are cheapest to complete within the budget
the longest chain of dependent tasks, setting the minimum project time
the shortest sequence of tasks, which sets the longest possible project time
questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest path through the network, so its total duration is the minimum time the project can take. Tasks that can be delayed without affecting the finish date have float and are not critical.

questions.stem: A project has four tasks. A (3 days) starts first. B (4 days) and C (2 days) both follow A. D (5 days) starts only when B and C are finished. What is the critical path and its duration?
options: A-B-C-D, taking 14 days
A-B-D, taking 9 days
A-B-D, taking 12 days
A-C-D, taking 10 days
questions.explanation: Path A-B-D takes 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 days and path A-C-D takes 3 + 2 + 5 = 10 days, so the longer path, A-B-D, is critical. B and C run at the same time, so they are not added together.

questions.stem: In the same project (A 3 days; B 4 days and C 2 days both after A; D 5 days after B and C), how much float does task C have?
options: 4 days
5 days
2 days
0 days
questions.explanation: C must finish by the time B finishes, at day 7, but it can finish at day 5, so it can be delayed by 2 days without delaying D or the project. Critical tasks such as B have zero float.

questions.stem: A project's critical path is 12 days. A non-critical task with 2 days of float is delayed by 3 days. What happens to the project?
options: it finishes 3 days late, at 15 days
it still finishes on time, at 12 days
it finishes 2 days late, at 14 days
it finishes 1 day late, at 13 days
questions.explanation: The first 2 days of delay are absorbed by float, but the third day pushes that path past the critical path, so the project takes 13 days. A delay longer than a task's float makes it critical.

questions.stem: Why do managers focus most closely on critical tasks in critical path analysis?
options: critical tasks can be postponed until all others are finished
critical tasks are the only ones shown on a Gantt chart
any delay to a critical task delays the whole project
critical tasks are always the most expensive to complete
questions.explanation: Critical tasks have no float, so any delay to them delays project completion. Resources may be moved from non-critical tasks, which have float, to keep critical tasks on schedule.

questions.stem: Capacity utilisation is calculated as:
options: actual output / maximum possible output x 100
maximum possible output / actual output x 100
total costs / number of units produced
fixed costs / (selling price - variable cost)
questions.explanation: Capacity utilisation shows what percentage of maximum output is being produced. Total costs divided by units is cost per unit, and the last formula is break-even.

questions.stem: A Tamworth abattoir can process 10,000 animals a month but processes 7,500. What are its capacity utilisation and capacity cushion?
options: 75% utilisation and a 75% capacity cushion
133% utilisation and a 33% capacity cushion
75% utilisation and a 25% capacity cushion
25% utilisation and a 75% capacity cushion
questions.explanation: Utilisation = 7,500 / 10,000 x 100 = 75%. The capacity cushion is the unused capacity, 100% - 75% = 25%, which allows the business to meet sudden rises in demand.

questions.stem: A factory has fixed costs of $40,000 a month and variable costs of $5 per unit. What happens to cost per unit if output rises from 8,000 to 10,000 units?
options: it stays at $5 per unit
it falls from $10 to $5
it falls from $10 to $9
it rises from $9 to $10
questions.explanation: At 8,000 units, ($40,000 + $40,000) / 8,000 = $10; at 10,000 units, ($40,000 + $50,000) / 10,000 = $9. Higher utilisation spreads fixed costs over more units.

questions.stem: Which is a cost of a business being under capacity, unable to produce enough to meet demand?
options: lost sales and dissatisfied customers who go to competitors
idle equipment and staff that raise the cost of each unit
a large capacity cushion that is expensive to maintain
warehouses full of unsold stock that may become obsolete
questions.explanation: When capacity is too low, orders go unfilled, overtime costs rise and customers may switch to rivals. Idle equipment and a large cushion are costs of being over capacity.

questions.stem: A Dubbo factory has run at 55% capacity for two years, and demand is forecast to stay low. Which capacity decision is most appropriate?
options: buy more equipment so that the factory can lower its cost per unit
hire more permanent staff to raise the factory's capacity utilisation
build a second factory to gain economies of scale over its rivals
sell or lease out some equipment to reduce the cost of unused capacity
questions.explanation: Long-term over capacity means paying for idle assets, so selling or leasing them out reduces costs. Buying more equipment would make utilisation even lower.

questions.stem: In operations management, economies of scale are achieved when:
options: cost per unit falls as the scale of production increases
total costs fall as the scale of production increases
selling prices rise as more units are produced
variable costs disappear as more units are produced
questions.explanation: Larger scale allows bulk buying, specialised equipment and fixed costs spread over more output, so the average cost of each unit falls. Total costs still rise with output.

questions.stem: A product sells for $50, its variable cost is $30 per unit and fixed costs are $60,000. How many units must be sold to break even?
options: 750 units
3,000 units
1,200 units
2,000 units
questions.explanation: Break-even point = fixed costs / (price - variable cost per unit) = $60,000 / $20 = 3,000 units. Dividing by the price instead of the contribution of $20 gives 1,200 units.

questions.stem: Using the same figures (price $50, variable cost $30, fixed costs $60,000), what is the profit if 4,000 units are sold?
questions.explanation: Each unit contributes $20, so 4,000 units contribute $80,000; subtracting fixed costs of $60,000 leaves a profit of $20,000. Equivalently, the 1,000 units above break-even each add $20.

questions.stem: A business's break-even point rises after its rent increases. This is because:
options: higher fixed costs need more units sold to be covered
higher fixed costs raise the contribution of each unit
higher variable costs lower the price of each unit
higher rent reduces the number of units it can make
questions.explanation: Break-even = fixed costs / contribution per unit, so a rise in fixed costs such as rent means more units must be sold before profit is made. Rent does not change the contribution per unit.

questions.stem: A NSW government upgrade of a major highway cuts travel time to Sydney for a Hunter Valley manufacturer. This political influence on operations is:
options: a WHS requirement, which sets safety rules for drivers
an environmental regulation, which limits truck emissions
infrastructure, which can lower transport costs and lead times
a trade policy, which places a tax on imported inputs
questions.explanation: Government spending on infrastructure such as roads, rail and ports affects how quickly and cheaply inputs arrive and products reach customers. A tariff on imports would be a trade policy.

questions.stem: During a boom in the business cycle, an operations manager is most likely to:
options: cut shifts and reduce inventory of finished goods
close production lines that are running at full capacity
increase output and capacity to meet rising demand
sell equipment because demand is expected to fall
questions.explanation: Rising demand in a boom calls for more output, extra shifts and possibly more capacity. Cutting shifts and selling equipment are typical responses to a contraction.

questions.stem: A manufacturer is considering robotic welding to replace manual welders. Which statement best weighs this process technology innovation?
options: it will not affect other functions, because process technology concerns operations only
it may lower unit costs and improve consistency, but has high set-up and training costs
it will remove every operations cost, because robots do not need any maintenance
it will increase flexibility at no cost, because robots can make any product at once
questions.explanation: New process technology can raise speed, quality consistency and efficiency, but it involves large upfront costs, staff training or redundancies and the risk of the technology dating. It affects human resources and finance as well as operations.

questions.stem: Under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW), a business conducting operations must:
options: ensure that all workers are paid at least the national minimum wage
ensure that its products carry a warranty against all defects
ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, workers' health and safety
ensure that no worker ever works more than 38 hours in any week
questions.explanation: The Act places a primary duty of care on a person conducting a business or undertaking to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, workers' health and safety. Hours and minimum wages are set under workplace relations law, not WHS law.

questions.stem: How do work health and safety requirements influence operations decisions?
options: they require all businesses to use a fixed-position layout for safety
they shape layout, equipment and procedures to reduce harm
they set the prices a business may charge for goods made in a factory
they decide how many units a business must produce to break even
questions.explanation: WHS duties lead managers to design safe layouts, guard machinery, train staff and set safe procedures, which can add costs but reduce injuries and lost time. No particular layout type is required by law.

questions.stem: A business sold 3,000 units this quarter and 90 were returned as faulty. What is its product return rate?
questions.explanation: Product return rate = returned units / units sold x 100 = 90 / 3,000 x 100 = 3%. A rising return rate signals quality problems.

questions.stem: A Coffs Harbour distributor made 480 deliveries last month, of which 456 arrived on time. Its target on-time delivery rate is 98%. Which statement is correct?
options: its rate is 95%, which is above target, so it can cut delivery staff
its rate is 95%, which is below target, so it should investigate delays
its rate is 105%, which is above target, so no action is needed
its rate is 5%, which is far below target, so it should change carriers
questions.explanation: On-time delivery rate = 456 / 480 x 100 = 95%, below the 98% target, so managers should find the causes of late deliveries. The 5% figure is the late rate, not the on-time rate.

questions.stem: Production lead time is best described as:
options: the time a machine can run before it needs maintenance
the number of units produced in each hour of operation
the time taken for a new product to reach maturity
the time between receiving an order and completing the product
questions.explanation: Production lead time measures how long it takes to produce an order, so shorter lead times support the speed objective. Units per hour is a measure of output rate.

questions.stem: A factory's cost per unit has risen 12% over a year while the industry benchmark has stayed steady, and capacity utilisation has fallen from 85% to 60%. Which corrective action best targets the cause?
options: raise wages for all staff so that they are motivated to work more quickly
add a third shift so that the factory's maximum capacity becomes larger
lower the selling price, since cost per unit does not affect profitability
win extra volume or reduce unused capacity, so fixed costs are spread better
questions.explanation: Falling utilisation spreads fixed costs over fewer units, so cost per unit rises. Raising volume or cutting unused capacity addresses this; adding a shift increases capacity and makes utilisation worse.

questions.stem: Operations doubles output to cut cost per unit, but marketing has no plan to sell the extra stock and finance must borrow to fund it. What does this show?
options: operations decisions need to be aligned with other functions and strategy
operations decisions should always aim for the highest possible output
cost per unit is the only metric that matters in operations management
finance and marketing decisions do not depend on operations decisions
questions.explanation: Operations, marketing and finance are interdependent: extra output only helps if it can be sold and funded. Decisions within operations must fit the other functions and the business strategy.
